```{=html}
<div class="lx-interactive lx-cards" data-learn="grid-outages" data-src="../assets/learn/data/f06-grid-and-outages.json ../assets/learn/data/03-balancing.json ../assets/learn/data/path.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The idea in one table: eight stops from a power plant to a socket</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table f6-fbt">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Stop</th><th scope="col">Prairie Town (illustrative)</th><th scope="col">Typical in the U.S.</th><th scope="col">What it does</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>1 Generator</td><td>18 kV</td><td>5–34.5 kV</td><td>Makes alternating current</td></tr>
<tr><td>2 Step-up transformer</td><td>18 → 345 kV</td><td>up to 115–765 kV</td><td>Raises the voltage for the long trip</td></tr>
<tr><td>3 Transmission line</td><td>345 kV</td><td>115–765 kV</td><td>Carries power far, in loops</td></tr>
<tr><td>4 Substation</td><td>345 → 12.47 kV</td><td>down to below 34 kV</td><td>Steps down; breakers protect each feeder</td></tr>
<tr><td>5 Distribution feeder</td><td>12.47 kV</td><td>4.8–34.5 kV</td><td>Runs through the streets; laterals reach each block</td></tr>
<tr><td>6 Service transformer</td><td>12.47 kV → 240/120 V</td><td>240/120 V</td><td>Steps down for a few homes</td></tr>
<tr><td>7 Service drop and meter</td><td>240/120 V</td><td>240/120 V</td><td>Brings power into the home and counts the kWh</td></tr>
<tr><td>8 Socket</td><td>120 V</td><td>120 V (240 V for big appliances)</td><td>Powers the lamp</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Then a storm on Prairie Town's east side (30 homes, illustrative)</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table f6-fbt">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">What failed</th><th scope="col">Device that opened</th><th scope="col">Homes dark</th><th scope="col">Repair</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>A branch on Oak Street's lateral</td><td>Its fuse</td><td>6</td><td>2 h</td></tr>
<tr><td>A limb on the north feeder's far half</td><td>Recloser R1</td><td>10</td><td>3 h</td></tr>
<tr><td>A snapped pole on the south feeder</td><td>The south feeder's breaker</td><td>10</td><td>6 h</td></tr>
<tr><td>A toppled tower on one line of the high-voltage loop</td><td>None: power goes round the loop</td><td>0</td><td>12 h, by a separate crew</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>
<ul>
<li><b>Losses.</b> Sending 100 MW through a 5-ohm line loses 10.5% at 69 kV but 0.42% at 345 kV: five times the voltage, one twenty-fifth of the loss. All U.S. lines and wires together lose about 5% (2018 through 2022).</li>
<li><b>Repairs.</b> One crew, best order: north feeder's far half, then Oak Street, then the south feeder, for 10,200 customer-minutes.</li>
<li><b>Measures.</b> The storm's SAIDI is 10,200 ÷ 30 = 340 minutes; its SAIFI is 26 ÷ 30 = 0.87 interruptions per customer.</li>
<li><b>The real U.S.</b> In 2025 the average customer had 269.2 minutes without power and 1.34 interruptions, or 125.3 minutes without major event days. Over 90% of interruptions start on the distribution system.</li>
</ul>
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you work through this step by step: the path, a voltage slider, a network you can break, a storm, a repair order and the real U.S. numbers.</p>
</div>
</div>
<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span><b>Real data.</b> Voltage classes from DOE's <a href="https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2023-11/FINAL_CESER%20Electricity%20Grid%20Backgrounder_508.pdf">grid backgrounder</a> (November 2023, p. 2) and <a href="https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2017/01/f34/Electricity%20Distribution%20System%20Baseline%20Report.pdf">distribution baseline report</a> (2016, pp. 27, 38). Losses: <a href="https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=105&amp;t=3">EIA</a> (updated 7 November 2023). Reliability: <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_11_01.html">EIA, Electric Power Annual, Table 11.1</a> (released 21 October 2026), utilities using the IEEE 1366 method.<br><b>Illustrative.</b> Prairie Town's voltages within those ranges, its east-side network and 30 homes, the 5-ohm line, the storm and its repair hours.</span></p>
<p class="lx-hint" style="margin-top:10px">Need a refresher? <a href="03-balancing.html">Lesson 3</a> keeps the grid balanced second by second; <a href="f01-five-scales.html">F1</a> places feeders and microgrids on the five scales.</p>
```
:::

::: {#explain .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="f6-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Voltage steps</dt><dd><span class="lx-term" data-term="transformer">Transformers</span> raise the voltage from 5–34.5 kV at the plant to 115–765 kV for <span class="lx-term" data-term="transmission">transmission</span>, then lower it in steps to 240/120 V at the home.</dd>
<dt>Why high voltage</dt><dd>The same power at a higher voltage needs less current, and the heat lost in a wire grows with current squared.</dd>
<dt>Meshed and radial</dt><dd>Transmission lines form loops, so one can fail and power goes round; most feeders are radial, with one path to each home.</dd>
<dt>Protection</dt><dd>A fault opens the closest fuse, <span class="lx-term" data-term="recloser">recloser</span> or breaker upstream of it, darkening only the section below it.</dd>
<dt>SAIDI and SAIFI</dt><dd><span class="lx-term" data-term="saidi">SAIDI</span> is customer-minutes without power ÷ customers served; <span class="lx-term" data-term="saifi">SAIFI</span> is customers interrupted ÷ customers served.</dd>
<dt>Where outages start</dt><dd>Over 90% of U.S. interruptions start on the <span class="lx-term" data-term="distribution">distribution</span> system, mostly in bad weather (DOE, 2017).</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>SAIDI, SAIFI, CAIDI and major event days</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Utilities report three yardsticks to EIA each year (Form EIA-861). All three count only non-momentary interruptions.

| Yardstick | What it measures | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| [SAIDI]{.lx-term term="saidi"} | Minutes without power, per customer, in a year | minutes |
| [SAIFI]{.lx-term term="saifi"} | Interruptions per customer in a year | interruptions |
| [CAIDI]{.lx-term term="caidi"} | Average minutes to restore one interruption: SAIDI ÷ SAIFI | minutes |

A [major event day]{.lx-term term="major-event-day"} (IEEE 1366) is a day whose SAIDI exceeds a threshold set from the past five years of daily values. Reports give the yardsticks with and without them:

| U.S., IEEE method | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| SAIDI, all events | 662.6 min | 269.2 min |
| SAIDI without major event days | 131.6 min | 125.3 min |
| SAIDI, loss of supply removed | 646.1 min | 246.8 min |
| SAIFI, all events | 1.531 | 1.34 |
| SAIFI without major event days | 1.065 | 1.08 |

Source: [EIA, Electric Power Annual 2025, Table 11.1](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_11_01.html) (released 21 October 2026). The minutes without major event days stay near two hours a year; the stormy days swing the total.

- **Try it.** CAIDI for 2025: 269.2 ÷ 1.34 = 201 minutes per interruption.
- **Read with care.** Utilities that do not use the IEEE method decide their own major events, so EIA gives the IEEE group on its own and all utilities together ("any method").

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>N−1 as a rule in a network model</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The loop survives any one failed line: the [N−1]{.lx-term term="n-minus-one"} idea. A planning or operating model writes it as a rule for each possible outage.

- **Decisions.** Which plants run, and how much power each line carries.
- **Rules.** For each line $k$ that might fail, the flows that remain must still fit every other line's limit: one copy of the network rules per outage.
- **What it costs.** With $L$ lines, the model grows from one network to $L + 1$ networks.

[M1](m01-dispatch-to-lmp.html) builds the network rules for one case; Analyst lesson A17 (upcoming) checks a plan against grid physics, and A9 (upcoming) plans for hazards.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Three phases and alternating current: real power flow also needs voltage and reactive power (Analyst lesson A17, upcoming).</li>
<li>Protection settings: how fast each fuse, recloser and breaker acts, so the closest one opens first.</li>
<li>Momentary interruptions: a recloser that trips and closes again within seconds, which SAIDI does not count.</li>
<li>Underground cables, rooftop solar pushing power back up a feeder, and switches that reroute feeders.</li>
<li>Crews, travel time, parts and priority loads such as hospitals: this lesson's crew weighs only the number of homes.</li>
<li>Supply: the network checks only connection; keeping supply equal to demand is <a href="03-balancing.html">lesson 3</a>.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

::: {#check .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Practice, about 10 minutes: three myths, then six questions.</p>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="f6-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="plants" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Most power outages start at power plants.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. DOE found that over 90% of U.S. power interruptions start on the distribution system, mostly in bad weather (2017). Plant and transmission failures are rarer, but can darken many customers at once.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="voltage" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A higher-voltage line wastes more energy.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. For the same power, a higher voltage needs less current, and the heat lost falls with the square of the current: five times the voltage, one twenty-fifth of the loss.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="blink" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “SAIDI counts every flicker of the lights.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. EIA's SAIDI counts non-momentary interruptions only. A recloser that trips and closes again within seconds, after a branch brushes a wire, causes a momentary one.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="f6">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="saidi" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">A utility serves 10,000 customers. A fault darkens 400 of them for 90 minutes. How much does it add to the year's <span class="lx-term" data-term="saidi">SAIDI</span>?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">3.6 minutes</li><li data-value="b">36 minutes</li><li data-value="c">90 minutes</li><li data-value="d">0.04 minutes</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>3.6 minutes: 400 × 90 = 36,000 customer-minutes, ÷ 10,000 customers. Its SAIFI share is 400 ÷ 10,000 = 0.04 interruptions per customer.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="fuse" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A branch falls on a lateral that has its own fuse. What opens?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">The substation transformer</li><li data-value="b">The lateral's fuse</li><li data-value="c">The feeder's breaker at the substation</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>The lateral's fuse: the closest device upstream of the fault opens, so only the homes on that lateral go dark.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="double" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">Double the line's voltage and send the same power. What happens to the heat lost in the wire?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">It doubles</li><li data-value="b">It halves</li><li data-value="c">It falls to a quarter</li><li data-value="d">It stays the same</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>A quarter: the current halves, and the loss goes with current squared, (½)² = ¼.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="socket" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">Which voltage does a typical U.S. wall socket give?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">120 V</li><li data-value="b">12.47 kV</li><li data-value="c">345 kV</li><li data-value="d">5 V</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>120 V. Homes get 240/120 V service; 12.47 kV is a common feeder voltage, and 345 kV a transmission voltage.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="loop" data-answer="d">
<p class="lx-qtext">In the lesson's high-voltage loop, one of the three lines falls. How many homes go dark?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">All 30</li><li data-value="b">10</li><li data-value="c">6</li><li data-value="d">None</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>None: power takes the other way round the loop. Only when both lines into the substation fall do all 30 homes go dark.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="med" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">In 2025, U.S. SAIDI was 269.2 minutes with major event days and 125.3 minutes without them. About what share came on major event days?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">About 47%</li><li data-value="b">About 53%</li><li data-value="c">About 27%</li><li data-value="d">About 215%</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About 53%: (269.2 − 125.3) ÷ 269.2 = 0.53. In 2024, a year of hurricanes, it was about 80%.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::
